title: Weeping Higan Cherry: Shidarezakura You Can Visit
meta_description: A cherry whose flowering branches hang straight down. Miharu's Takizakura, over a thousand years by tradition, draws 300,000 people a year.
intro: Shidarezakura hang their flowering branches straight down, so the tree makes a curtain you walk under rather than a canopy you look up into, and they open before the ordinary somei-yoshino. The greatest is the Miharu Takizakura in Fukushima, the waterfall cherry, put at over a thousand years by tradition, its crown 22 metres across; around 300,000 people a year come to stand under it. In the hills of Yamanashi, Shinden no Oitozakura told Kobuchisawa's farmers when to plant rice before calendars did. Kyoto's famous ones are often stand-ins, and nobody minds. The weeping cherry everyone photographs at Maruyama Park is the second one on the spot. The Taiko cherry at Daigo-ji is not the tree Toyotomi Hideyoshi saw at his enormous blossom party of 1598, but it stands where the party happened. In Nara, the local spring is dated from the cherry beside the approach to Himuro Shrine.
